sections.h2: What rights do Minnesota tenants keep when the landlord sells the building?
sections.html: Minnesota's landlord and tenant rules sit in Chapter 504B, and several of them speak directly to a sale. The deposit has to move or be returned, the new owner steps into the old owner's deposit duties, and the landlord's right to bring buyers through the unit is limited by a notice rule.

sections.h2: What happens to the security deposit when a Minnesota rental is sold?
sections.html:
Within 60 days after the landlord's interest ends, or sooner if the buyer must account for the deposit to the tenant, the seller has to do one of two things under Minn. Stat. 504B.178, subdivision 5. The seller can transfer the deposit, with interest and any lawful deductions, to the buyer and then tell the tenant about the transfer and the buyer's name and address. Or the seller can return the deposit with interest to the tenant.

The buyer takes over the landlord's rights and duties for the deposit. If the tenant does not object to the stated amount within 20 days after written notice, the buyer's obligation is limited to the amount in the notice. That notice must include a stamped envelope addressed to the buyer and may go by mail or personal service. Deposits earn simple interest at one percent a year.

The penalties are real. A landlord who fails to transfer or return the deposit as required owes the tenant an amount equal to the portion withheld, plus interest, on top of the wrongly held deposit. Bad faith retention adds punitive damages up to $500 per deposit, and failing to follow the transfer or return rules creates a presumption of bad faith unless the money is returned within two weeks after a lawsuit starts.

sections.h2: How fast must a Minnesota landlord return a deposit at move-out?
sections.html:
The landlord has three weeks after the tenancy ends to return the deposit with interest or send a written statement of the specific reasons for withholding. When a tenant leaves because of a legal condemnation that the tenant did not cause, the period is five days. Both clocks start after the landlord receives the tenant's mailing address or delivery instructions.

The landlord may withhold only amounts reasonably needed to cover unpaid rent or other agreed charges, or to restore the unit to its condition at the start of the tenancy, apart from ordinary wear and tear. In any dispute, the landlord carries the burden of proving the reason for each deduction.

  • Under Minn. Stat. 504B.182, the landlord must tell the tenant at move-in, or within 14 days, about the option of an initial inspection.
  • Before move-out the landlord must offer a move-out inspection no earlier than five days before the lease ends, if the tenant asks for one.
  • A tenant may not skip the last month's rent and call the deposit payment. Doing so creates a rebuttable presumption and can bring a penalty and interest under subdivision 8.

sections.h2: Can a landlord show a Minnesota rental to a buyer?
sections.html:
Yes, and the statute names it. Minn. Stat. 504B.211 lists showing the unit to a prospective buyer as a reasonable business purpose for entry. The landlord must still make a good faith effort to give reasonable notice of at least 24 hours, the notice must name a time or window, and entry is allowed only between 8:00 a.m. and 8:00 p.m. unless both sides agree otherwise.

Emergencies are the exception. A landlord who reasonably suspects that immediate entry is needed to prevent injury or property damage, to check a tenant's safety, or to comply with local ordinances may go in without notice. If the tenant is not home and no notice was given, the landlord must leave a written disclosure of the entry in a conspicuous place.

A violation can bring a rent reduction up to full rescission of the lease, return of the damage deposit less lawful deductions, a civil penalty of up to $500 per violation and attorney fees. The same section treats a violation as a breach of the landlord covenants in 504B.161.

sections.html:

sections.h2: What repairs and conditions must a Minnesota landlord provide?
sections.html:
Minn. Stat. 504B.161 writes several covenants into every residential lease, and the parties cannot waive or modify them. The landlord promises that the premises and common areas are fit for use, kept in reasonable repair, including pest extermination, reasonably energy efficient, and in compliance with health and safety laws and local rental licensing rules. The landlord must also supply heat of at least 68 degrees Fahrenheit in all habitable spaces, kitchens and bathrooms included, from October 1 through April 30.

A landlord can ask a tenant to handle specific repairs only through a conspicuous written agreement supported by adequate consideration, and that agreement cannot waive these covenants or relieve the landlord of common area upkeep. Tenants facing an emergency can petition the court under Minn. Stat. 504B.381. Listed emergencies include a serious infestation, loss of water, heat or electricity, and a government condemnation.

Retaliation is barred. Under Minn. Stat. 504B.441, a landlord may not evict a tenant, raise obligations or cut services as a penalty for a complaint, and if the move comes within 90 days of the complaint the landlord has to prove otherwise.

sections.h2: How does eviction work for unpaid rent in Minnesota?
sections.html:
Before a landlord files for nonpayment, Minn. Stat. 504B.321 requires a written notice stating the total due, an itemized accounting of rent, late fees and other charges, the name and address of the person authorized to receive payment, and the legal help and financial assistance statements set out in the statute. The landlord delivers it personally or by first class mail. If the tenant does not pay or vacate within 14 days, or a longer period set by local rule, the landlord may file.

The court appearance is set not less than seven nor more than 14 days after the summons is issued. If the landlord wins, the court enters judgment and issues a writ of recovery of premises. Under Minn. Stat. 504B.345, the court generally stays that writ for a reasonable period not to exceed seven days, except in actions based on certain serious conduct or when a default judgment was entered. A tenant who wins gets judgment, costs and expungement of the court records.

Grounds for eviction, listed in Minn. Stat. 504B.285, include a holdover after the lease term ends, after rent becomes due under the lease terms, or after notice ending a tenancy at will. A landlord cannot bring an eviction solely because the tenant was a victim of violence or after the tenant ended the lease under Minn. Stat. 504B.206.

sections.h2: What special situations change the rules for a rented home?
sections.html:
Some circumstances shorten or lengthen the usual periods. A lease other than a tenancy at will can be ended after the tenant's death, by the landlord or the tenant's personal representative, with two months written notice effective on the last day of a calendar month. The tenant's estate stays liable for rent owed before and during that period.

  • Tenants who fear imminent violence after domestic abuse, criminal sexual conduct, sexual extortion or harassment may end a lease with signed written notice and a qualifying document, and the landlord must keep the information private or face $2,000 in statutory damages plus fees.
  • A tenant whose lease began during a mortgage redemption period may be entitled to 90 days written notice from the successor after foreclosure, and landlords who learn of a foreclosure sale may only sign short leases under Minn. Stat. 504B.151.
  • To enforce an automatic renewal clause, the landlord must send a written reminder 15 to 30 days before the tenant's notice deadline.

Owners who would rather not manage a sale around tenants, showings and deposits can ask for an as-is cash offer on a Minnesota rental and set the closing date and the handling of the deposit in the purchase agreement.

faqs.q: What happens to my security deposit if my Minnesota landlord sells the building?
faqs.a: The landlord must either transfer the deposit with interest to the buyer and notify you, or return it to you, within 60 days of the sale or when the buyer must account to you, whichever comes first. The buyer then holds the landlord's duties for it, and you have 20 days from the written notice to object to the stated amount.

faqs.q: Can my Minnesota landlord show my home to buyers without asking me?
faqs.a: Only after a good faith effort to give at least 24 hours of reasonable notice, naming a time or window between 8:00 a.m. and 8:00 p.m. unless you agree to something else. Emergency entry is allowed without notice when the landlord reasonably suspects an immediate danger to people or property.

faqs.q: How long does a Minnesota landlord have to return a deposit?
faqs.a: Three weeks after the tenancy ends, or five days after a legal condemnation you did not cause, once the landlord has your mailing address. The landlord must return the deposit with interest or send a written statement of the specific reasons for any deduction.

faqs.q: How much notice does a Minnesota landlord give before filing an eviction for unpaid rent?
faqs.a: A written notice with the amount due and an itemized accounting, and then 14 days, or a longer local period if the city or county requires one. If you pay the full amount or move out in that time, the landlord cannot file on that notice.

faqs.q: Can a Minnesota landlord evict me for complaining about repairs?
faqs.a: No. A landlord may not evict, raise your obligations or cut services as a penalty for a complaint. If it happens within 90 days of the complaint, the landlord must prove it was not retaliation. After 90 days, you carry the burden.
